name: Marco Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so please tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a usual day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, 43, and lead the incident-reporting software team at a tech company. I have a master's degree and know the clients' safety workflows, but the part I care about is keeping a worker's own account with the incident when our code sends it for review. I don't use AI tools. My partner teaches mathematics, and we have two children at school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small sorter may group routine incident reports, but the worker's own words must stay attached. I do not use AI tools; I compare the filed report with the signed account before changing our software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tools stay small, my work and household money feel secure. I lead the incident-reporting team at a tech company, earn a high developer wage, my partner teaches mathematics on steady hours, we have about nine months of expenses saved, and many software firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing the incident portal and ask the client safety officer about reports marked closed too soon. In the first year we'd save another 200 each payday while both wages hold; I'd make sure the sorter never deletes the original worker statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A person should be able to read what they said after the software has filed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a summary get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worker reported that a machine guard was loose, but the summary called it a housekeeping issue. The signed statement and a photograph showed why the machine guard needed inspection before the case closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about incident records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children know I do not talk about people's injuries at dinner. I tell them a record should help someone fix a hazard, not turn a worker into a number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI writing code, classifying reports and answering workers could make our team smaller before anyone admits it. I would ask our staff association to bring safety officers and workers into the review of the new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep my lead post because I know the clients, but I could lose part of my team and eventually paid hours. Nine months saved would support a search, yet other firms may use the same tools; I do not want a worker's own account lost in an efficiency claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the association to request a joint meeting with client safety officers and a written record of reports AI closes wrongly. If our firm trials AI triage in the first year, I'd keep checking a sample of closed cases against signed worker statements; we would postpone replacing the family car until the staffing plan is written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the job and angry about closed cases that hide hazards. A good salary does not make a worker's missing account acceptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which incident should the trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loose-guard case should be in the error set. I'd ask the safety officer whether the guard was inspected before the AI marked the report resolved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What purchase would you delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I had discussed a newer car, but the current one runs. We can wait until the company says who is still paid to review reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches incident code and report decisions before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. Workers still need a person to hear an appeal when a hazard is marked safe wrongly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my software post could be cut if a cheap system writes and checks the whole portal. Nine months saved and my partner's teaching wage make the shock survivable for a while, but a wide change could close many developer openings together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd put safe examples of bad closures into a work record and ask the staff association to jointly demand notice and paid appeal roles before layoffs. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real paid safety-case posts with authority to reopen reports and a household wage covering mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd use savings for a wider search and ask the association whether an emergency fund exists, without budgeting it before approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can afford a search for a time, but I expect the job I trained for to become cheap very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would a new safety role need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A safety-case role would need written authority to send the guard report back for inspection. I would not accept a title where I can only watch a queue of closed reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that our house is not on the market today. My partner and I would check actual wages before deciding anything that changes their school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives firms time to put a person in charge of disputed hazard closures. Robots follow around 2034, but thinking AI reaches our code and reports first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might earn by reviewing disputed cases if clients pay for that review, but I cannot call it a job just because someone writes the title on a chart. My software post could still shrink. Nine months of savings give us room to negotiate, not permission to work for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our association to seek a written paid-review clause in the next client contract, with a safety officer able to reopen cases. If the client signs and the firm assigns paid work hours, I'd take that role; in the first year after 2031 I'd stay only while the contract funds the hours and my wage still covers mortgage and school costs, otherwise I'd apply for real paid software posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the future of my own wage, though I can negotiate from a stronger position than someone with no savings. I would not use AI myself just because a client wants a cheaper queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paid clause actually give a worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clause would say a worker can ask for a second look and a named safety officer signs the decision. I would show the loose-guard case as the reason for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if management offers only a title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management offers a review title without paid hours, I'd stay on my present work while it lasts and ask the association to bring the issue back to the client. A title without hours is not a job for our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives us time to keep a worker's report and the reason a hazard was closed in the same place. Thinking AI reaches report code in 2036, while hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be doing paid appeals work or still building software. Our high wages and nine-month cushion make the next few years secure, but I would not count a future client contract before it is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loose-guard case log and check that worker statements stay attached to corrections. We'd save 200 each payday while both wages hold, and join the association yearly in requesting paid appeal roles in client renewals; in the first year after 2036 I'd move only for a signed job whose combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our current money. I can argue for fair review without telling my children their home is at risk tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful case log show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The log would show the worker's words, the guard photograph and the reopened decision, with names removed. I want future developers to see how a report changed, not only a green resolved badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your child about future work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child asks whether computer jobs will stay. I'd tell them to learn useful work and ask who bears the cost of a bad system, then look at real paid places when they choose a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because code and incident triage could change before workers have a paid person to hear appeals. Notice before cuts, written authority to reopen cases and funded paid review work would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a closed incident is the same as a fixed hazard. The worker who reported a loose guard deserves to know who inspected it, not just receive a green resolved badge.

headlineQuote: The worker who reported a loose guard deserves to know who inspected it, not just receive a green resolved badge.
